papers.title: Eccentricities and inclinations are decoupled in super-Earth systems
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31617v1

summary.one_liner: Using N-body and secular simulations of four equal-mass super-Earths with uneven spacing, the paper tests whether the eccentricity and inclination Angular Momentum Deficit (AMD) components are approximately conserved quantities in stable low-mass multiplanetary systems.
summary.plain: Planets orbiting a star slowly exchange energy and tilt over very long times. This paper asks whether two summary measures of that motion, one tied to how stretched the orbits are and one tied to how tilted they are, stay nearly constant over billions of orbits. The authors simulated sets of four similar-sized "super-Earth" planets and found that, in stable cases, these measures change by typically less than 1%.
summary.why: If these measures are nearly constant, they could serve as a simple way to link the current layout of observed planetary systems to how they formed. The text does not show how far this holds beyond the single template family of four equal-mass planets studied here, so its wider reach remains to be tested.
summary.background:
- Planetary systems: a star with several planets on orbits that gently perturb each other.
- Secular dynamics: slow, long-term changes in orbit shape and tilt, averaged over the fast orbital motion.
- Eccentricity: how stretched an orbit is (0 is a circle).
- Inclination (mutual): how tilted one planet's orbital plane is relative to another's.
- Angular Momentum Deficit (AMD): a combined measure of orbit stretching and tilting that is conserved in the absence of collisions or ejections, so it is used as a check on dynamics.
- Quasi-integral of motion: a quantity that is nearly, but not exactly, constant over time.
- Lyapunov time: how quickly nearby trajectories diverge; short values indicate chaos.
- Ergodic: a system that eventually visits all of its possible states; the paper suggests this may not hold here.
- N-body simulation: direct numerical tracking of every body's motion; secular code: a faster, averaged approximation.

papers.abstract: Recent work on the longterm evolution of the inner Solar System has shown that the inclination contribution to the Angular Momentum Deficit (AMD) is almost constant even though inclinations and eccentricities are highly coupled in expansions of the perturbing function. We wish to characterize the conservation of the eccentricity AMD and inclination AMD, respectively describing the average eccentricity and mutual inclination of planetary orbits, beyond the case of the Solar System. We aim at showing that this conservation is a general feature of the stable planetary systems dynamics, in particular, in the context of low mass multiplanetary systems. We perform a series of numerical simulations using both N-body and secular codes to study the dynamics over billions of orbits. Taking as a template four equal mass Super-Earth with non uniform orbital spacing, we consider sets of systems with different AMD and use the orbital elements evolution to assess the conservation of inclination and eccentricity AMD components. For stable systems, the inclination AMD and eccentricity AMD relative variation is typically below 1%, making them quasi-integrals of motion. At low AMD, despite short Lyapunov timescales, the secular diffusion is confined and the dynamics almost quasi-periodic. As the AMD increases, the emergence of large scale secular chaos only weakly affects the conservation of the quasi-integrals, which breaks when systems become fully unstable. The eccentricity and inclination evolution (as measured by the variation of their AMD contributions) are largely decoupled for low mass multiplanetary systems. Combined with the weak diffusion of the Laplace-Lagrange modes at low AMD, these findings paint a picture where the secular dynamics are not necessarily ergodic. The uncovering of these quasi-integrals opens a new path to relate the observed planetary architecture to its formation.

papers.title: The Jupiter ICy moons Explorer (JUICE) Mission: Post-Launch Status and Mission Overview
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31467v1

summary.one_liner: A post-launch status report and mission overview for ESA's JUICE spacecraft, which is cruising toward Jupiter to study the icy moons Ganymede, Europa and Callisto, the Jupiter system, and related targets.
summary.plain: This is a progress report on a European space probe, JUICE, that launched in April 2023 and is still travelling to Jupiter. It describes what the mission plans to do once it arrives in 2031: fly past three large icy moons that likely hide liquid water oceans under their surfaces, then go into orbit around Ganymede. The text sets out goals rather than new measurements, since the spacecraft has not yet reached its target.
summary.why: The mission asks whether conditions that could support life exist in the oceans of moons beyond Earth, a question that bears on the wider search for habitable worlds. The text itself reports no results yet, so its value lies in documenting the plan and instruments for later findings.
summary.background:
- JUICE is a European Space Agency (ESA) mission, the first large mission in its Cosmic Vision long-term science programme.
- Jupiter has four large "Galilean" moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. The three icy ones are Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
- Scientists think these icy moons have liquid water oceans beneath their surfaces, which is why they are of interest for habitability.
- Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System and has its own magnetic field.
- A magnetosphere is the region around a planet shaped by its magnetic field; the paper also mentions the thermosphere and ionosphere, the upper atmosphere layers.
- The payload is 10 instruments plus a radio experiment using the spacecraft's communication link with ground radio telescopes.

papers.abstract: The JUpiter ICy Moons Explorer (JUICE) is the first large-class mission in ESA's Cosmic Vision programme. Proposed in 2007 and selected in 2012, it was launched on 14 April 2023 from Kourou and is now en route towards Jupiter. After arrival in July 2031, JUICE will spend approximately four years studying the Jupiter system, performing multiple flybys of three of its Galilean moons, the icy moons Ganymede, Europa, and Callisto, before entering orbit around Ganymede for its final year. The mission will investigate conditions that may support habitable environments within the satellites, all of which are thought to contain subsurface liquid water oceans. Ganymede, the largest moon in the Solar System, is a prime target due to its internal structure and possible subsurface ocean, its unique intrinsic magnetic field, and its complex interactions with Jupiter's magnetosphere, offering a natural laboratory for studying the emergence, evolution and potential habitability of icy worlds around giant planets. JUICE will also conduct a global investigation of the Jupiter system as the archetype for gaseous giant planet systems: it will study Jupiter's atmospheric circulation, composition, and flow of energy from the cloud tops to the thermosphere and characterise the 3D structure of the magnetosphere and its coupling with the ionosphere and thermosphere. Interactions between the moons and the magnetosphere, as well as tidal and gravitational evolution within the Galilean system, will also be assessed. Additional science objectives include the innermost Galilean moon, Io and its neutral cloud and plasma torus, some small inner and irregular moons, and the ring systems. The payload includes 10 instruments and one experiment using the spacecraft's telecommunications system to connect with ground-based radio telescopes, plus an onboard radiation monitor.

papers.title: From residuals to warps: Probing disk geometry with gas kinematics
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31408v1

summary.background:
- Protoplanetary disks: gas and dust disks around young stars, where planets may form.
- Keplerian disk: a disk whose gas orbits in the simple pattern set by gravity; deviations from this pattern carry information about the disk's shape.
- Inclination and position angle: how tilted the disk is to our line of sight and its orientation on the sky.
- Warp: a change in tilt or orientation with distance from the star, so the disk is not flat.
- Shadows: dark bands in scattered light caused by parts of a warped disk blocking starlight.
- CO rotational line emission observed with ALMA: radio light from carbon monoxide molecules, used to trace gas motion via Doppler shifts.
- Radiative transfer simulation: computing how light travels through and is emitted by a modeled object.
- Spectral resolution: how finely velocities are resolved in the data.
summary.one_liner: Using CO line kinematics from synthetic radiative-transfer maps, this paper tests when residuals from a Keplerian disk model can recover the three-dimensional warp shape of protoplanetary disks, and where the method fails.
summary.plain: Young stars are often surrounded by spinning disks of gas and dust that may be bent out of flat, like a warped record. Measuring that bend from light is hard because a warp can look much like other features, such as shadows. The authors simulated disks with known bends, produced fake telescope maps of carbon monoxide gas, and checked how well a simple method could recover the bend from how the gas moves.
summary.why: Warps may shape how disks evolve and where planets form, and shadows cast by warped disks have been seen in observations, so a reliable way to measure warps matters. The text reports the method works for nearly face-on disks with small warps but breaks down at high inclinations, high emission heights, and sharp transitions, so its use on real disks is still limited.

papers.abstract: Evidence of shadowing among protoplanetary disks suggests that warped protoplanetary disks are widespread, making it crucial to constrain their three-dimensional shape in order to understand their dynamical evolution and origin. Yet, inferring this warp shape from observations is challenging, as the typical signatures of a warp, especially shadows, are often degenerate with the warp shape. Kinematics of disks may provide a method to recover the shape by interpreting the residuals from a Keplerian disk model as local changes in inclination and position angle. In this work, we test its applicability and limitations. We perform radiative transfer simulations of disks with a parametrized warp shape to create synthetic maps of $^{12}\mathrm{CO}$ rotational line emission at ALMA wavelengths and compare the fitted warp with the true warp shape. We find that the warp shape can be recovered for nearly face-on disks with small warp misalignments of a few degrees, even without knowledge about disk properties such as emission height. The overall warp shape remains traceable even at moderate spectral resolutions up to $0.8\,\mathrm{km/s}$. However, we identify regimes where the method breaks down, including disks with an inclination higher than $40^\circ$, a high emission height of the tracer, and sharp warp transitions. In addition, radial and vertical motions can introduce apparent warps and twists, motivating extensions of the method to account for these effects.

papers.title: Kepler-404: A near-resonant pair of sub-Neptunes. Reinterpreting a false-positive signal with the novel detection method RIVERS.radon
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32298v1

summary.background:
- Transit method: a planet crossing its star dims the starlight slightly; the dips reveal the planet.
- Transit timing variations (TTVs): when planets gravitationally perturb each other, their transits arrive earlier or later than a fixed schedule.
- Resonance: two planets whose orbital periods form a simple whole-number ratio (here near 5:4), so they regularly tug on each other.
- Signal-to-noise ratio: how strong a signal is relative to random noise; low values make detection hard.
- Photodynamical fit: a model that simulates the gravitational dynamics and the light curve together to estimate planet masses and radii.
- False positive: a signal flagged as a planet candidate that later turns out to come from something else.
- Kepler mission: NASA telescope whose light curves are the data source here.
summary.one_liner: The paper shows that transit-timing variations can hide low-signal planets from standard transit searches, and uses a new 2D cross-correlation detector (RIVERS.radon) to recover Kepler-404b from a false-positive flag, finding it in a near 5:4 resonance with Kepler-404c and fitting both planets' radii and masses.
summary.plain:
Planets that pass in front of their star cause tiny regular dips in its brightness, and a planet's own gravitational tugs on its neighbour can shift those dips in time, which makes standard searches miss faint signals. The authors built a new search method that does not assume the dips arrive on a strict schedule, and applied it to the star Kepler-404. They found that a signal previously labelled a false positive is a real planet, and that it and a companion planet orbit in a near-resonant pattern with similar size and mass.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Near-resonant planet pairs are expected to be common by planet-formation theory, yet few are observed, and this work suggests detection bias from timing shifts may partly explain the gap. The link to that broader population question is the paper's own argument; the text alone does not show how general the bias is.

papers.abstract: According to the current understanding of planet formation and evolution, (near)-resonant systems should be a common occurrence in nature. However, pairs of planets with period ratios close to commensurability are rarely observed. In this paper, we discuss how observational bias caused by transit timing variations (TTVs) can affect the detection of low signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) planets in transit surveys, playing a role in the lack of representation of these systems. We present an alternative detection method, RIVERS.radon, which overcomes the effect of TTVs on planet detectability by not relying on an exact periodic solution for the transit signal. It leverages 2D representations of the light curve and approximates the transits with a set of local periodic solutions with the use of 2D cross-correlation. We present an application of RIVERS.radon to the near-resonant system Kepler-404, showing that the signal of the false-positive candidate KOI-2768.03 belongs to the planet Kepler-404b and that it is in a near 5:4 resonance with its companion Kepler-404c, causing TTVs of amplitudes 117.64 and 110.09 minutes, respectively. With a photodynamical fit, we retrieve a pair of similar planets, respectively of radii $1.68^{+0.09}_{-0.09}$ and $1.69^{+0.10}_{-0.10}\,R_\oplus$ and of masses $1.91^{+0.41}_{-0.33}$ and $2.34^{+0.47}_{-0.40}\,M_\oplus$. We find that these planets exhibit typical (near)-resonant features: their densities are lower than the bulk population of exoplanets, and their orbits are nearly coplanar. Interestingly, the planets are found outside the resonance but at a significant distance from the equilibrium point of the $(X_{\rm res}, \delta)$ plane of the Hamiltonian, which is consistent with post-disk instability but somewhat at odds with the observed coplanarity.

papers.title: Shifting the snow line in protoplanetary disks by planet-induced multiple spiral shocks
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30158v1

summary.background:
- Snow line: the distance from a star where water vapor condenses into ice; it marks where icy solids become abundant.
- Protoplanetary disk: the rotating disk of gas and dust around a young star from which planets form.
- Accretion heating (Joule heating): warming of gas as it falls inward; recent magnetized simulations found this is weak, so the snow line may lie inside 1 au.
- Spiral shock: a shock wave in the gas, launched by a planet's gravity, that heats gas as it passes.
- Optical depth and opacity: how well the disk traps heat; higher opacity means heat escapes less easily.
- Hydrodynamical simulation: a computer model of gas flow that ignores magnetic fields.
- Entropy jump: a measure of how much a shock irreversibly heats gas.
- Jupiter-mass units: the planet here is about one-third of Jupiter's current mass.
summary.one_liner: Two-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations and a thermal-balance model show that spiral shocks driven by a giant planet can heat the inner disk enough to move the snow line (the radius where water ice forms) beyond 1 au, for a planet of about one-third Jupiter's mass at 5 au and an assumed opacity of 1 cm²/g.
summary.plain: Young planets form in thin disks of gas and dust around newborn stars. The "snow line" is the distance from the star inside which water is too warm to freeze, and where it sits affects whether rocky planets like Earth can form and keep their water. This paper asks whether shock waves in the disk, created by a growing giant planet's spiral arms, can heat the inner disk enough to push that line outward. The authors find that they can, when the planet is massive enough and the disk is dense enough to trap heat.
summary.why: Recent simulations had suggested the snow line might sit inside 1 au, which would make it hard to build Earth-like planets in place. If shock heating from a giant planet keeps the snow line farther out, it offers a physical route to forming rocky planets with water without special water-removal steps; the text suggests this may apply to the early formation of Jupiter in our solar system, though this is a model-based result.

papers.abstract: The snow line location provides important constraints on rocky planet formation. Recent magnetohydrodynamical simulations suggest that Joule heating associated with gas accretion is so inefficient that the snow line can be located inside 1 au around a solar-type star. This challenges in-situ formation of the terrestrial planets in the solar system unless other internal heating processes are present. Previous studies have proposed that spiral shocks induced by an embedded planet potentially shift the snow line outward. In this study, we investigate the impact of shock heating induced by a giant planet on the location of the snow line in two steps. First, we perform two-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations of a disk with a giant planet to model shock heating rates. We construct an empirical formula for total entropy jumps due to multiple spiral shocks interior to the planetary orbit. Second, we calculate the radial temperature profile based on the thermal balance with the modeled shock heating rates. We find that shock heating can substantially increase the disk temperature in inner regions far from the planet when the planetary mass and disk optical depth are sufficiently high. For example, assuming a fixed surface density profile and an opacity of $\kappa = 1~\rm cm^2\,g^{-1}$, a planet with one-third of Jupiter's current mass at 5 au can shift the snow line outward beyond 1 au. Our results suggest that the early formation of proto-Jupiter in the solar nebula may have enabled rocky planetesimals and protoplanets to form in the present-day terrestrial planet region without invoking additional water removal processes.

papers.title: Constraining Planet Nine with Pulsar Timing: Orbit Determination Method from the Acceleration, Jerk, and Snap of the Solar System Barycenter
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28471v1

summary.background:
- Planet Nine: a hypothesized planet far beyond Neptune, proposed to explain clustered orbits of distant trans-Neptunian objects.
- Solar system barycenter: the center of mass of the Sun and planets; it wobbles as planets orbit.
- Millisecond pulsar: a rapidly spinning neutron star whose radio pulses arrive with extremely steady timing.
- Pulse times of arrival and timing residuals: measured differences between when pulses are expected and when they actually arrive.
- Acceleration, jerk, snap: the first, second, and third time-derivatives of position (rate of change of acceleration and higher orders), which appear as progressively finer timing signatures.
- Orbit determination: inferring an object's orbit and mass from its gravitational effects.
summary.one_liner: A method for using timing variations of millisecond pulsars to constrain the mass and orbit of a hypothesized distant Planet Nine via the acceleration, jerk, and snap of the solar system barycenter, with a check against Uranus and Neptune.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether a possible large, unseen planet beyond Neptune, called Planet Nine, could be detected by how it tugs the solar system's center of mass. The idea is to watch very regular radio pulses from spinning neutron stars (millisecond pulsars) and look for tiny, systematic shifts in their arrival times. The authors show which kinds of timing changes are needed to pin down the planet's orbit, and they test the method by estimating the masses of Uranus and Neptune.
summary.why: Planet Nine is proposed to explain why several distant small icy bodies cluster in their orbits, but it has not been observed, so a independent detection route would be valuable. The text says the method could be used after an optical detection to weigh such a planet, but it does not show that pulsar data are currently precise enough to find one.

papers.abstract: Planet Nine is hypothesized to exist in the outer solar system in order to explain the physical orbital clustering of several trans-Neptunian objects. A Planet Nine would systematically change the location of the solar system barycenter (SSB). Therefore, the precise timing properties of millisecond radio pulsars would measure the acceleration, jerk, and snap of the currently-perceived SSB under the gravitational influence of a Planet Nine. We present a method on how to use pulsar spin frequency derivatives and binary pulsar orbital period derivatives to constrain the Planet Nine parameter space. We find that searches for unidentified massive objects in the solar system require at least cubic and quartic variations in the pulse times of arrival (corresponding to jerk and snap, respectively) in order to uniquely constrain an orbit. Otherwise, additional assumptions are required to fully constrain the mass and orbital parameters of the object. We use our method to weigh the ice giants Uranus and Neptune and obtain results consistent with the literature. This method could be used to weigh a Planet Nine after a putative optical detection. Future work will use updated pulsar timing datasets that benefit from longer observational baselines and advances in statistical modeling and noise characterization.

papers.title: Hints of planet formation in progress around DR Tau from observations with LBT SHARK-NIR and SHARK-VIS
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27643v1

summary.background:
- Protoplanetary disk: a rotating disk of gas and dust around a young star, where planets form.
- Embedded planet: a planet still growing inside its disk, usually much harder to see than a finished planet.
- Accretion: material falling onto a young object; hot falling gas emits specific colors of light, here hydrogen Halpha (visible red) and Paschen-beta (near-infrared).
- Narrow-band vs broad-band filters: narrow filters isolate one emission line; broad filters capture a wider color range.
- Signal-to-noise (S/N): how strong a signal is relative to background noise; S/N of 6 to 13 is a modest detection.
- Keplerian rotation: orbital motion expected for objects around a star, with inner parts moving faster than outer parts.
- MJup: Jupiter masses, a unit of planet mass.
- SPHERE: a previous high-contrast imager on the European VLT telescope that first detected the disk features.
summary.one_liner: High-contrast narrow-band and broad-band imaging of the DR Tau protoplanetary disk with LBT SHARK-VIS and SHARK-NIR finds two compact features, consistent with reflected starlight rather than confirmed Halpha or Pabeta accretion from an embedded planet.
summary.plain: Young stars are surrounded by disks of gas and dust where planets form, and astronomers want to directly see newborn planets still inside them. This paper looks at one such disk, around the star DR Tau, using two cameras on a large telescope in Arizona. The team found two faint compact spots that have persisted over seven years and may move like objects orbiting the star, but the light they emit appears to be starlight bounced off dust rather than the glow of a forming planet.
summary.why: Direct detections of forming planets are rare, so candidate sources in disks matter for testing how planets form. This paper is a useful but tentative step: its main result is that the spots are most likely reflected dust light, so the planet interpretation remains unconfirmed.

papers.abstract: Protoplanetary disks are the primary sites of planet formation. However, the direct imaging of protoplanets still embedded within their parental disks remains a significant challenge, with only a small number of confirmed detections to date and several candidates awaiting verification. We search for embedded planets in the protoplanetary disk of the young star DRTau by targeting accretion signatures from forming sub-stellar objects. Using narrow-band imaging, we observe both visible Halpha and near-infrared Paschen-beta (Pabeta) emission to identify actively accreting companions. To this end, we performed high-contrast observations of DRTau using the SHARK-VIS (0.40-0.95 micron) and SHARK-NIR (0.96-1.70 micron) imagers at the LBT. The study uses a combination of narrow-band filters to isolate accretion signatures and broad-band filters for multi-wavelength characterization in both the visible and near-infrared. Our observations recover the primary disk structures previously identified in the literature, albeit at low signal-to-noise (S/N). We identify two compact features with S/N between 6 and 13 in both narrow- and broad-band filters. The first, an elongated structure, matches previous SPHERE detections, while the second, more compact feature, is now confirmed despite its low S/N in earlier datasets. A comparison over a seven-year baseline confirms the stability of both structures. Their observed orbital motion is consistent with Keplerian rotation, potentially suggesting the presence of an undetected planetary-mass companion (few MJup) at the location of the second feature. However, our analysis does not confirm Halpha or Pabeta emission originating from localized accretion. Instead, we conclude that the observed flux is likely stellar light reflected by dust at these locations and discuss alternative mechanisms that could account for such detections.

papers.title: 2026 QQ8: Earth's temporary flyby of maximum lunation
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27770v1

summary.background:
- Temporary captures: a small asteroid can orbit Earth for a limited time before escaping, unlike the Moon, which is permanently bound.
- Astrometry: measuring precise sky positions over time to work out an orbit.
- Photometry and spectrophotometry: measuring brightness and colour across wavelengths; an "S-type" asteroid is a stony class, as opposed to darker carbon-rich types.
- Solar radiation pressure: the small push sunlight exerts on an object, which depends on its shape and density; here it helps separate natural from artificial objects.
- Orbit of maximum lunation: an orbit geometry, tied to the Moon's influence, where capture lasts longest.
- Discovery is recent, so the text gives no long-term follow-up.
summary.one_liner: Astrometric, photometric and dynamical study of asteroid 2026 QQ8, a natural temporary Earth companion on a long flyby orbit near the theoretical maximum-duration "orbit of maximum lunation," with solar radiation pressure used to rule out an artificial origin.
summary.plain: Sometimes a small asteroid is briefly pulled into orbit around the Earth and then drifts away again. This paper examines one such object, 2026 QQ8, which was recently discovered. The authors tracked its position and brightness, modelled its path, and checked how sunlight pushes on it, concluding it is a natural rock rather than man-made debris.
summary.why: It is only the third known temporary Earth companion on a flyby orbit and the first of long duration, and its orbit sits near the predicted upper limit for how long such a capture can last in the Earth-Moon system. This makes it a useful test case for models of how Earth captures and releases small bodies; the text does not go beyond this.

papers.abstract: Aims: On a rare occasion, asteroids are temporarily captured by the Earth to become the planet's interim companions. The discovery of asteroid 2026~QQ$_8$ provided an opportunity to study this class of objects, adding to the sparse discovery catalogue of Earth's temporary companions. Methods: We performed astrometric, photometric, and dynamical studies of 2026~QQ$_8$, and measured its solar radiation pressure signal to discern between a natural and an artificial origin. Results: We find 2026 QQ$_8$ to be of natural origin, with solar radiation pressure signal commensurable with natural objects and spectrophotometry of an S-type object. 2026 QQ$_8$ is Earth's third discovered otemporarily-captured companion on a flyby orbit, and the first long-duration one, owing this to being on the so-called "orbit of maximum lunation". Its unusual orbit lies close to the theoretical upper duration limit of an object captured in the Earth-Moon system, and has now been observed for the first time.

papers.title: IGRINS-2 Reveals an Oxygen-rich Dayside Atmosphere of WASP-12 b: Resolving the C/O Controversy
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27082v1

summary.background:
- Hot Jupiter: a gas giant planet orbiting very close to its star, with a surface hot enough to glow.
- Ultra-hot Jupiter: a hotter class of these planets, often above about 2,000 K.
- Dayside emission spectroscopy: splitting the light from the planet's sunlit side, measured when it is hidden behind its star, into colors to see which molecules are present.
- Cross-correlation: a method that searches the noisy spectrum for the known pattern of a specific molecule, summing many lines to boost a faint signal.
- C/O ratio: the relative amount of carbon and oxygen in the atmosphere; it hints at where the planet's building material formed.
- R/V ratio: refractory (rock-forming, hard-to-vaporize elements) compared with volatile material; here reported relative to the host star.
- Thermal inversion: a layer where temperature rises with altitude, so emission lines appear rather than absorption lines.
- Bayesian retrieval: fitting a physical atmosphere model to data while tracking uncertainties in its parameters.
- Sigma (σ): a measure of how unlikely a result is by chance; higher means more confident.
summary.one_liner: High-resolution near-infrared dayside emission spectroscopy of the ultra-hot Jupiter WASP-12 b with IGRINS-2 detects H2O, CO, and tentative OH and refractory signals, and a chemically consistent retrieval gives C/O = 0.72 (+0.08/−0.10), favoring an oxygen-rich dayside.
summary.plain: This paper studies the atmosphere of WASP-12 b, a very hot gas giant planet orbiting a star, which has been disputed for its carbon-to-oxygen balance. The authors used a high-resolution infrared spectrograph on the Gemini North telescope to capture light from the planet's day side after it passes behind its star. They report that the light carries fingerprints of water and carbon monoxide, and their modeling favors an oxygen-rich atmosphere.
summary.why: The carbon-to-oxygen ratio is a clue to where a planet's gas came from during formation, so settling a long-running disagreement about this planet matters for planet-formation theory. The text reports that the result disfavors carbon-rich solutions at greater than 5 sigma, but the signals for OH and refractories are only tentative, and the sample of similar planets is small, so the broader implications remain uncertain.

papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that measurements of hot-Jupiter atmospheric composition, including carbon-to-oxygen (C/O) and refractory-to-volatile (R/V) abundance ratios, provide powerful diagnostics of the chemistry and formation of gas giant planets. Important questions remain about the atmospheric composition of the ultra-hot Jupiter WASP-12 b: its dayside C/O ratio remains under debate, and its R/V ratio is not yet well constrained. We present high-resolution (R $\sim$ 45,000) near-infrared dayside emission spectroscopy of the ultra-hot Jupiter WASP-12 b with IGRINS-2 on Gemini North during post-eclipse phases. Cross-correlation analysis reveals volatile molecular signals of H$_2$O and CO together with tentative signals of OH and gas-phase refractories in the planetary atmosphere. The planetary signals appear in emission, indicating a thermal inversion in the dayside atmosphere. A chemically consistent Bayesian retrieval yields C/O $=0.72^{+0.08}_{-0.10}$, disfavoring carbon-rich dayside solutions with C/O $>1$ at greater than $5σ$. This independent, line-resolved measurement supports an oxygen-rich atmosphere, providing a new constraint on the long-standing C/O controversy surrounding WASP-12 b. Our retrieval also yields a host-star-normalized R/V ratio, $[\mathrm{R/V}]_{*}=0.17^{+0.22}_{-0.23}$, which is consistent with those of other ultra-hot Jupiters similarly characterized with IGRINS/IGRINS-2. Although the sample remains small, this consistency suggests a shared atmospheric chemistry among these planets, potentially reflecting similar proportions of accreted volatile and refractory material.

papers.title: Physics-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement of Amortized Bayesian Inference Across Physics
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27006v1

summary.background:
- Bayesian inference: estimating the probability distribution of unknown parameters given data (the "posterior").
- Posterior: the set of plausible parameter values, with their relative likelihoods.
- Likelihood: how probable the observed data are under a given set of parameters.
- Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC): a standard, often slow, sampling method for posteriors; "converged chains" means runs that have settled into reliable sampling.
- Amortized inference: a neural network is trained once on simulations so that later posteriors for new data come almost instantly.
- Importance weights: correction factors that reweight approximate samples to match the exact likelihood.
- Equation of state: the relation between pressure and density in dense matter such as neutron-star interiors.
- Recursive self-improvement: an AI system iteratively revising its own methods based on feedback.
summary.one_liner: PhyRSI uses an AI agent tied to physics simulators to repeatedly rewrite amortized Bayesian inference code for six fields, with each version scored by importance-weighted exact likelihoods because the true posterior is unknown.
summary.plain: Scientists often infer hidden physical parameters, such as an exoplanet's orbit or a neutron star's internal matter, from noisy measurements, and the standard computer methods for this can be very slow. This paper describes an AI system that writes and revises its own fast inference method for each field, and the physics itself is used to check whether the results are right. Once trained on simulations, the networks return posteriors (the range of likely parameter values) for 36 real observations in seconds.
summary.why: The text reports that the fast posteriors, after reweighting by the likelihood, agree with converged Markov chains about as well as two independent chains agree with each other, which is a useful benchmark for speed-versus-accuracy claims. It suggests possible uses in real-time control of thin-film growth and patch-clamp experiments, following X-ray transients, and updating neutron-star equation-of-state constraints, but these applications are proposed in the text rather than demonstrated, and the broader significance is not yet established.

papers.abstract: Across physics, from the orbits of imaged exoplanets and the matter inside neutron stars to thin films at synchrotrons and cortical neurons, conservation laws, interference, and compensating currents compress the posteriors of precise data into tiny, curved regions where Markov chains need minutes to days. We introduce PhyRSI (physics-guided recursive self-improvement), in which an AI agent coupled to the simulator writes and revises an amortized Bayesian inference algorithm for each field, scored by the importance weights of the exact likelihood because the true posterior is unknown. It evolves coordinates, symmetries, and factorizations matched to the physics: orbital elements at the best-measured epoch, Fresnel-normalized reflectivity with a chart for each of its multiple solutions, coordinates along which Na+ and K+ currents compensate, a shared neutron-star equation of state that factorizes a 32-dimensional joint analysis, and the time-rescaling symmetry of predator-prey dynamics. In six fields, networks trained once on simulations return 36 posteriors of real observations in seconds, reweighted by the likelihood and agreeing with converged Markov chains about as closely as two independent chains agree with each other. Such posteriors could steer synchrotron film growth and patch-clamp recordings as they run, follow X-ray transients while they are bright, update the dense-matter equation of state as neutron stars are added, and compare physical models across catalogs. Inference can thus be evolved and checked by the physics itself rather than designed by hand for each problem.

papers.title: Dependence of Dust Growth on Magnetic field Strength in Protoplanetary Disks
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25602v1

summary.background:
- Protoplanetary disk: a rotating disk of gas and dust around a young star, where planets form.
- Dust growth: tiny grains stick together (coagulation) or shatter on collisions (fragmentation).
- Radial drift: gas pressure makes dust slowly spiral inward toward the star, capping how large grains can get.
- Magnetorotational instability (MRI): a process in which a weakly magnetized, rotating gas becomes turbulent, which transports angular momentum and stirs dust.
- Plasma beta: ratio of gas pressure to magnetic pressure; a smaller value means a stronger field relative to gas pressure.
- Non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics: effects (ambipolar diffusion, Ohmic dissipation) by which weakly ionized gas lets magnetic fields drift or decay.
- One-dimensional calculation: the model varies along only one coordinate (here, distance from the disk midplane or radius, as simplified in the model), not a full 3D simulation.
summary.one_liner: A one-dimensional study coupling dust coagulation and fragmentation with the evolution of a vertical magnetic field, including ambipolar diffusion and Ohmic dissipation, to test how magnetorotational-instability-driven turbulence sets dust growth in protoplanetary disks.
summary.plain: This paper looks at how the magnetic field inside a young, gas-and-dust disk around a newborn star affects how small dust grains clump into larger particles, the raw material for planets. The authors ran computer simulations in which the dust sizes and the magnetic field evolve together, and the turbulence the field stirs up is calculated from the field's own strength. They found that a stronger magnetic field (a lower "plasma beta," a measure of how much gas pressure compares with magnetic pressure) makes the turbulence stronger, which helps dust grow in the regions where it is active.
summary.why: The result suggests that magnetic turbulence matters for dust growth mainly in the outer disk, while inward radial drift (dust spiraling toward the star) still limits the maximum grain size over most of the disk. This is relevant to understanding how planetary building blocks form, though the text describes only a one-dimensional model, so its broader applicability is uncertain.

papers.abstract: We performed one-dimensional calculations to investigate how the magnetorotational instability (MRI) affects dust growth in protoplanetary disks. We simultaneously solved the evolution of the dust size distribution and the vertical magnetic field. The dust size distribution is evolved taking into ac- count coagulation and fragmentation. For the magnetic field evolution, we considered both ambipolar diffusion and Ohmic dissipation. The MRI-driven turbulent viscosity was estimated self-consistently from the local magnetic field strength and non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics diffusivities. We found that MRI-driven turbulence becomes stronger for smaller initial plasma beta, and the enhanced tur- bulence promotes dust growth in MRI-active regions. However, dust growth is ultimately limited by radial drift, and the dependence of dust size on the magnetic field strength is significant only in the outer regions of the disk. In other words, over most of the disk, radial drift remains the dominant factor controlling the maximum dust size, and the magnetic field strength plays only a minor role in determining the overall dust size distribution.

papers.title: The Effect of Dust Grain Growth and Stellar Metallicity on Gas Giant Planet Formation by Disk Instability
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26804v1

summary.background:
- Protoplanetary disk: a rotating disk of gas and dust around a young star, where planets form.
- Gravitational instability: when a disk's self-gravity overcomes its internal pressure and forms dense clumps that can contract into planets.
- Toomre criterion: a stability measure for rotating disks; lower values mean the disk is more prone to clumping.
- Opacity: how strongly material blocks radiation; dust grains raise opacity, slowing cooling.
- Grain growth: small dust particles clumping into larger ones, which changes opacity.
- Metallicity: the fraction of elements heavier than helium in a star; solar metallicity is the Sun's value.
- Jupiter mass (M_Jup) and astronomical unit (au): units for planet mass and orbital distance.
summary.one_liner: Three-dimensional radiative hydrodynamics simulations test how lower dust opacity (from grain growth or sub-solar metallicity) affects gas giant planet formation by gravitational fragmentation of protoplanetary disks around solar-mass stars.
summary.plain: This paper asks how giant planets can form quickly from the gas around a young star by the disk breaking into clumps under its own gravity. Such clumps need the gas to cool fast enough, and cooling depends on how much the tiny dust grains in the gas block heat from escaping. The authors ran computer simulations with standard dust opacity and with opacity reduced by factors of 10 and 100, and found that lower opacity produced more fragmentation, but all cases formed clumps of similar mass and distance.
summary.why: It links grain growth and star chemistry (metallicity) to whether disk instability can make giant planets, a question of how planets like those seen in exoplanet surveys form. The text suggests the effect may matter most around metal-rich stars, but this is a modelling study of early clump evolution only, so its broader implications remain uncertain.

papers.abstract: The formation of gas giant planets by the gas disk gravitational instability (GDGI) mechanism depends sensitively on the thermodynamics of the protoplanetary disk gas: disk gas must be able to cool on orbital timescales for dense clumps to become gravitationally unstable and contract to form protoplanets. Since disk cooling is regulated by the opacity of the dust grains embedded in the gas, the properties of these dust grains are critical for the GDGI mechanism. Grain growth to larger sizes than assumed in traditional opacity models for solar metallicity, as well as protostars with sub-solar metallicity, should have lower opacity disks that are more conducive to planet formation by GDGI. Here we use a three dimensional radiative hydrodynamics and gravitation code to compute the evolution of the GDGI in $0.091 M_\odot$ disks with varied initial minimum values (1.3 to 2.7) of the Toomre criterion orbiting solar-mass protostars. Three sets of eight models are computed: one with the standard opacity, and two more with the opacity reduced by arbitrary factors of 10 or 100. As expected, the reduced opacity models result in enhanced disk fragmentation by the GDGI and the production of more self-gravitating clumps than the standard opacity models. Nevertheless, all three opacities form similar self-gravitating clumps at this early phase of clump evolution, with masses of 0.2 to 0.7 $M_{Jup}$ and semimajor axes between 6 and 13 au. Significant dust grain growth should enhance the ability of the GDGI to form protoplanets around super-solar metallicity protostars.

papers.title: Transition Zone from ExoEarth to ExoVenus: Critical Insight from Planets on the Edge
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25255v1

summary.background:
- Habitable Zone: the range of distances from a star where liquid surface water can in principle exist.
- Venus Zone / Venus Evolution Zone: closer-in orbits where a planet is more likely to lose its water and develop a runaway greenhouse climate.
- Transition Zone: the overlap between these two, where planets may be either Earth-like or Venus-like.
- Exoplanet Archive: a NASA catalogue of confirmed planets around other stars; Gaia DR3 is a European Space Agency star-mapping data release used to refine stellar properties.
- JWST: the James Webb Space Telescope, which can analyse planetary atmospheres.
- Exo-Venus / exo-Earth: planets around other stars that resemble Venus or Earth.
summary.one_liner: The paper builds a target list of 23 rocky exoplanets in an "Earth-to-Venus Transition Zone" (plus 2 in the Venus Evolution Zone), using NASA Exoplanet Archive data updated with Gaia DR3, and assesses their demographics and follow-up observing potential.
summary.plain: Earth and Venus are similar in size and mass but ended up with very different climates, and scientists want to know why. This paper proposes studying rocky planets around other stars that sit between the zone where Earth-like water can persist and the zone where Venus-like conditions likely occur. The authors compiled a list of 23 such planets, plus 2 in the Venus zone, to help astronomers choose which ones to observe.
summary.why: Such planets could test how starlight strength affects whether a planet keeps its surface water, and could offer evidence about Venus's past that complements future Venus missions. The text presents this as a planning and target-selection tool; whether these observations will settle the Earth–Venus question is not shown here.

papers.abstract: Venus and Earth, planets with similar masses and radii, provide astonishingly different environments, raising the question of why these two rocky worlds evolved so differently. Explaining this divergence is a central challenge in comparative planetology and astrobiology. Now, atmospheric studies of exoplanets can explore the possibilities of terrestrial planet evolution, especially in the era of JWST; however, we have not yet realized the critical insights rocky exoplanets in the Transition Zone (TZ) can provide. These TZ planets in the overlap between the Habitable Zone and Venus Zone can test how incident stellar irradiation affects surface water retention and habitability. Observations of exoplanets in the TZ can probe not only the emergence and decline of exoplanet habitability but also test hypotheses about Venus' past, complementing upcoming Venus flagship missions. Here, we analyze NASA's Exoplanet Archive, updated with Gaia DR3 data, and provide a target list of 23 rocky exoplanets in the Earth-to-Venus Transition Zone, along with 2 planets in the Venus Evolution Zone (EV). We examine their demographics and quantify their potential for follow-up observations. This list of rocky TZ and EV planets allows observers to optimize target selection and observing strategy for specific instruments. Characterizing exoplanets in the Transition Zone will be critical to investigating open questions about the emergence and decline of habitability on rocky worlds, the evolution from an exo-Earth to an exo-Venus, and Earth's future.

papers.title: NEXONN: Advancing the NEXOTRANS Exoplanet Atmospheric Retrieval Framework with Transformer-Based Neural Posterior Estimation for JWST Transmission Spectroscopy of WASP-39b
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23818v1

summary.background:
- Transmission spectroscopy: measuring how much starlight passes through a planet's atmosphere at different wavelengths, which reveals its chemistry.
- Atmospheric retrieval: working backwards from a measured spectrum to the most likely atmospheric composition and temperature, with uncertainties.
- Bayesian posterior: the range of plausible parameter values, with probabilities, consistent with the data.
- C/O ratio: the balance of carbon to oxygen in the atmosphere, relevant to how the planet formed.
- [M/H]: a measure of how metal-rich the atmosphere is compared with the Sun.
- Neural posterior estimation: training a neural network on simulations so it can produce these probability ranges quickly once trained.
- Normalizing flow and transformer: types of neural network architectures used for this task.
- JWST instruments (NIRISS, NIRSpec, MIRI): infrared instruments aboard the telescope that cover different wavelength ranges.
summary.one_liner: NEXONN applies a transformer-conditioned normalizing-flow neural posterior estimator within the NEXOTRANS retrieval framework to infer WASP-39b's atmospheric properties from JWST transmission spectra, benchmarked against PyMultiNest.
summary.plain: Astronomers try to work out what a distant planet's atmosphere is made of by analysing the faint dimming of starlight as the planet passes in front of its star. The standard method of doing this is slow, so this paper builds a machine-learning tool that gives similar answers in seconds. The authors test it on simulated data and on real James Webb Space Telescope observations of the planet WASP-39b.
summary.why: Faster analysis could make it practical to study many planets at once, which is needed to understand how planets form and change over time. The text reports close agreement with the standard method on most parameters but also notes some parameter-dependent differences, so the tool's reliability is still being assessed rather than settled.

papers.abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope is delivering unprecedented constraints on exoplanet atmospheres, but computationally intensive Bayesian retrievals challenge the transition from individual planets to population-level studies of planetary formation and evolution. We introduce NEXONN, a transformer-conditioned normalizing-flow framework within NEXOTRANS that enables rapid atmospheric posterior estimation with uncertainty quantification. Incorporating PandExo-based JWST noise, we benchmark NEXONN against PyMultiNest using simulated spectra and JWST observations of WASP-39 b (0.6-12 microns). For simulated MIRI/LRS data, eight posteriors achieve a mean overlap of 80.32%. Retrievals of combined NIRISS, NIRSpec, and MIRI observations yield consistent atmospheric properties. For the full dataset, NEXONN infers C/O = 0.82 (+0.01/-0.02) and [M/H] = 1.13 (+0.04/-0.04), compared with PyMultiNest values of 0.80 (+0.03/-0.01) and 1.19 (+0.05/-0.03). Divergence metrics, Wasserstein distances, posterior overlaps, and coverage tests assess posterior fidelity and uncertainty calibration, revealing parameter-dependent differences. Once trained, NEXONN performs posterior inference within seconds, enabling scalable population studies of exoplanet atmospheric composition, formation, and evolution.

papers.title: A novel method for dust evolution in protoplanetary disks and a new criterion for gap opening
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22913v1

summary.background:
- Protoplanetary disk: a rotating disk of gas and dust around a young star, where planets form.
- Dust gap: a ring-shaped region with little dust, often carved by a forming planet's gravity.
- ALMA: a radio telescope array that images these disks in detail.
- Stokes number (St): a measure of how strongly a dust grain is coupled to the gas; small St means small grains that move with the gas.
- Planet-to-star mass ratio (q): planet mass divided by star mass, a dimensionless size measure.
- Particle tracking vs. fluid modelling: following individual grains versus treating dust as a continuous fluid.
- FARGO3D: a widely used fluid simulation code for disks, used here as the reference.
- Residence time: how long a dust particle spends in a given region.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces the Grain Residence-Time Method, a particle-tracking shortcut that reconstructs steady-state radial dust profiles in protoplanetary disks, validates it against FARGO3D fluid simulations, and proposes an empirical criterion for dust gap opening as a function of planet-to-star mass ratio and Stokes number.
summary.plain: The paper is about how dust is distributed in the disks of gas and dust around young stars, where planets form. The authors built a faster computer method that tracks individual dust particles and works out how long they stay at each distance from the star, and then uses that to estimate the dust density profile without simulating the dust as a fluid. They report that it agrees very well with standard fluid simulations over a wide range of settings, and they use it to study when a forming planet carves a gap in the dust.
summary.why: Gaps in dust seen in ALMA images are often linked to planets, so a cheaper way to model them and a simple rule for when they open could help interpret observations. The abstract claims a new gap-opening regime for small grains and low planet masses, which may matter for those images, but the text given does not show how strongly this is supported beyond the authors' own parameter study.

papers.abstract: We present the Grain Residence-Time Method (GRTM), a computationally efficient particle-tracking approach for studying dust evolution and trapping in protoplanetary disks. By reconstructing steady-state dust distributions from particle residence times, this method provides a way to obtain radial dust surface density profiles without directly evolving the dust as a fluid. We compare the GRTM with dust profiles computed via standard methods using the $\texttt{FARGO3D}$ code, which models the dust as a pressureless fluid, and find very good agreement over a wide range of parameter space. Finally, we investigate how dust gap formation depends on the planet-to-star mass ratio ($q$) and Stokes number ($\mathrm{St}$), through a parameter study, establishing an empirical criterion for dust gap opening. In doing so, we have discovered a new regime of gap opening for small grains with $St \lesssim 10^{-2}$ and for planet mass well below Jupiter's, which is likely very relevant for gaps seen in ALMA images.

papers.title: Observational diagnostics of external photoevaporation at millimetre wavelengths
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22952v1

summary.background:
- Protoplanetary disks: rotating disks of gas and dust around young stars, where planets may form.
- Photoevaporation: heating and blowing away disk gas by ultraviolet or X-ray light.
- External photoevaporation: the stripping is driven by UV light from nearby massive stars, not by the host star.
- FUV field (G0): far-ultraviolet light strength, measured relative to the average interstellar background (G0 = 1).
- Molecular line emission: molecules such as CO, HCO+ and C2H emit radio light at specific frequencies when they change energy level; these are the "transitions" studied.
- ALMA: a millimetre/submillimetre radio telescope array in Chile.
- Thermochemical models: simulations that combine heating, cooling and chemistry to predict what molecules emit.
- Flux ratio: dividing one line's brightness by another's, which can cancel out shared effects such as stellar mass.
summary.one_liner: Using a large grid of thermochemical disk models, this paper predicts millimetre-wavelength ALMA line fluxes under external FUV fields of 100 to 100,000 G0 and identifies 135 line-flux ratios that could help diagnose external photoevaporation in spatially unresolved protoplanetary disks.
summary.plain: Young stars are often surrounded by disks of gas and dust that can be stripped away by ultraviolet light from nearby massive stars, a process called external photoevaporation. This paper uses computer models to predict how the radio signals from 48 molecular transitions in these disks would change with the strength of that outside light. It finds that single line brightnesses are confused by differences in the star and disk themselves, so the authors instead propose comparing pairs of lines, of which they identify 135 that look promising.
summary.why: Knowing whether a disk is being eroded by its neighbours matters for how quickly planets can form there, and this gives observers a concrete set of line ratios to test with ALMA. The text is based on modelling only, so how well these ratios work on real observed disks remains to be shown.

papers.abstract: External photoevaporation is increasingly recognised as an important influence on protoplanetary disk evolution. However, there are no established molecular line diagnostics that can reliably distinguish external irradiation from variations in intrinsic stellar and disk properties. We use a large grid of thermochemical models to predict the fluxes of 48 transitions from eight species observable with ALMA, spanning a wide range of system properties and external FUV fields of 100 to 100,000 G0. At fixed stellar and disk properties, all transitions generally brighten with increasing FUV field strength. HCO+ and CO fluxes increase monotonically in virtually all disks, whereas lower-excitation lines, particularly those of C2H and N2H+, respond weakly and non-monotonically. However, variations in stellar mass and disk size introduce substantial degeneracies, limiting the usefulness of individual line fluxes as tracers of external irradiation. We therefore assess all pairwise line flux ratios, which can significantly reduce these degeneracies, evaluating their correlation with the external field, the magnitude of their change across the FUV range, and predicted ALMA detectability. We identify 135 promising ratios, including several combining strong FUV sensitivity and high detectability with efficient single-tuning ALMA observations. The strongest diagnostics either contrast high- and low-excitation lines of the same or co-spatial species (e.g. CO J=8-7/J=1-0), probing different regions of the photoevaporative wind, or pair an FUV-sensitive wind tracer with comparatively insensitive emission arising closer to the disk (e.g. HCO+ J=3-2/C2H N=3-2). Our results provide a framework for identifying externally photoevaporating systems from spatially unresolved emission and constraining their incident FUV field strengths.

papers.title: Connecting Calcium Depletion and Dust Evolution in the Rapid Accretor T28
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21786v1

summary.background:
- T28 is a young star (a protostar still forming) in the Chamaeleon I star-forming cloud.
- Protoplanetary disk: a rotating disk of gas and dust around a young star, where planets form.
- Mass accretion rate: how fast the star pulls in gas from its disk.
- Calcium depletion: calcium is less abundant in the infalling gas than in the star's expected composition, likely because dust grains containing it were removed.
- Refractory material: rock-forming elements that condense at high temperatures and stick to dust.
- Pre-transitional disk: a disk with a gap separating an inner and outer ring of dust, often read as a sign of forming planets.
- Spectrograph and infrared excess: instruments that split light into colors; extra infrared light reveals warm dust around the star.
- Au (astronomical unit): the Earth–Sun distance.
summary.one_liner: A multi-wavelength study of the young star T28 in Chamaeleon I combines new MIKE optical spectra with archival infrared data to link its calcium depletion in accretion flows to its dust disk structure, which is modeled as a pre-transitional disk with a gap extending to 16 au.
summary.plain: This paper looks at a young star called T28 that is still pulling gas from a surrounding disk where planets may form. The authors found that the gas falling onto the star is unusually poor in calcium, and that the dust disk seems to have a gap that current telescope images would not resolve. They suggest this calcium shortage may be tied to how fast the star is feeding and to early giant planet formation, though the link is a proposal rather than a demonstrated result.
summary.why: Calcium depletion in accreting gas is a possible chemical fingerprint of planets locking up rocky material before it reaches the star, so the proposed link between accretion rate, disk mass, and early giant planet growth is worth watching. The authors present this as a possible explanation for a trend seen in their sample, and the single-object nature of the case study means it is a suggestive rather than settled connection.

papers.abstract: We present a multi-wavelength case study of the star T28 in the Chamaeleon I star-forming region and investigate the dust evolution of its highly Ca-depleted protoplanetary disk. We combine new observations from the MIKE spectrograph on the Magellan Clay Telescope with archival IRS spectrum and photometry. We constrain the optical extinction using the hydrogen column density of the region, and apply ROTFIT to obtain stellar parameters. We estimate the mass accretion rate by fitting the excess flux above the photosphere with an accretion shock model. We model the line profiles of Ca II K and H$α$ with magnetospheric accretion models to infer Ca/H abundance, while the infrared excess is modeled with irradiated accretion disk models to get disk properties. We find that T28 is a high accretor with significant Ca depletion in its accretion flows. We find that the disk is best fit with a pre-transitional model with a disk mass of 0.12 $M_{\odot}$, where two optically thick disks are separated by a gap filled with optically thin dust extending to 16 au. This gap would not be resolved in the existing observations. T28 follows the trend of increasing depletion with increasing mass accretion rate. This trend can potentially be explained by preferential and early giant planet formation in massive disks, as suggested by recent planet formation simulations, leading to enhanced capture of refractory material in the massive disks of high accretors and thus depletion in the material reaching the star.

papers.title: Complex Interplay between Outer Disk Dynamics and Inner Water Reservoir
papers.label: arXiv:2611.20617v1

summary.background:
- Protoplanetary disk: a rotating disk of gas and dust around a young star, where planets form.
- Snowline: the distance from the star beyond which water freezes into ice.
- Pebble drift: larger dust grains lose orbital energy and spiral inward, carrying ice with them.
- ALMA: a radio telescope array that measures millimetre-wavelength dust emission and gas (CO) emission.
- JWST/MIRI: the James Webb Space Telescope's mid-infrared instrument, used here to detect water vapour in the inner disk.
- Visibility fitting (frank): a way of modelling radio interferometer data directly to find ring and gap features.
- Astronomical unit (au): the Earth–Sun distance.
- Gap leakiness, grain size and thermal history: other factors the authors say also control inner-disk water.
summary.one_liner: A homogeneous survey of outer-disk dust and gas sizes and substructures for 51 protoplanetary disks, linked to JWST/MIRI inner-disk water diagnostics, finds no global correlation between cold-to-hot water flux ratio and single outer-disk parameters, but compact structureless disks show signs of unimpeded pebble drift.
summary.plain: This study looks at young planet-forming disks of gas and dust around stars and asks whether the outer part of each disk controls how much water reaches the inner, rocky-planet zone. The authors combined new radio observations (ALMA) with archived data for 51 disks, and matched them to infrared measurements of water from the JWST telescope. They found no simple overall link, but three small, smooth disks with very extended gas show the pattern expected if icy pebbles drift freely inward.
summary.why: Water delivered by drifting pebbles is one proposed route for putting water into forming planets, so tying it to measurable disk structure matters for planet-formation models. The text only supports a tentative link: it reports a few compact disks with a pattern consistent with pebble drift, and states that structured disks vary widely, so a clean rule is not established.

papers.abstract: We present a homogeneous characterization of outer disk dust and gas properties for 51 protoplanetary disks from the JWST/MIRI Cycle 1 programs, combining new ALMA observations with archival data. Visibility fitting with frank recovers more and higher-contrast substructures in the mm continuum than image-plane analysis, placing the innermost features of several disks at 4-5 au and leaving only three disks featureless at the current resolution. CO gas disk sizes span $\sim$60-1000 au and correlate strongly with mm continuum sizes, with $R_{\rm CO}/R_{\rm mm}$ ranging from 1.4 to 9.7 (median 2.95). We then connect these outer disk properties to JWST/MIRI inner disk water diagnostics. We find no global correlation between the cold-to-hot water flux ratio ($F_{\rm cold}/F_{\rm hot}$), a proposed proxy of cold water enrichment by pebble transport, and any single outer disk parameter, including $R_{\rm mm}$, $R_{\rm CO}/R_{\rm mm}$, and innermost substructure location. Three compact ($R_{\rm mm}<30$ au), structureless disks with $R_{\rm CO}/R_{\rm mm}>4$ show both elevated $F_{\rm cold}/F_{\rm hot}$ and cold water emission near the snowline temperature, consistent with unimpeded inward drift of icy pebbles. For structured disks, the water properties instead vary widely at fixed gap location, reflecting the sensitivity of the inner disk water content to multiple factors, including gap leakiness, grain size, and thermal history. Linking outer disk dust evolution to inner disk water content thus requires carefully selected samples with detailed constraints on these additional parameters.
